title: The development and evolution of Tbr2-positive cells in the vertebrate pallium
abstract: Abstract The mammalian neocortex is a highly complex, six-layered structure composed of diverse neuronal and glial cell types that support sensory processing, motor integration, and higher cognitive functions. Excitatory neurons originate from neural progenitors in the embryonic pallium, primarily within the ventricular and subventricular zones. Radial glial cells function as key NSCs, generating neurons directly or via intermediate progenitors, which act as transit-amplifying cells committed to neuronal differentiation. This review focuses on Tbr2-positive cells, widely used as markers for IPs, and summarize their characteristics, regulation, and evolutionary significance across species. Because Tbr2 expression is not necessarily restricted to intermediate progenitors across diverse species, the conventional assumption that Tbr2-positive cells are synonymous with IPs should be reconsidered in a comparative developmental context. Understanding the diversity, regulation, and evolutionary origins of Tbr2-positive cells will provide insights into the development and evolution of neocortical structure and neural progenitor diversity.
